newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Trade data sows doubts over S.Korean soft landing.
newsitem.headline: Trade data sows doubts over S.Korean soft landing.

text.p: South Korea's current account deficit jumped again in September, and high industrial inventories plus slowing consumption added to doubts about a soft landing for the economy, analysts said on Wednesday.
The Bank of Korea said the current account deficit expanded to $1.41 billion in September, almost double the $753.1 million shortfall in the same month of 1995.

In the first nine months the deficit hit $17.09 billion, more than double the $8.08 billion deficit a year earlier. The deficit is officially forecast to be $19 billion this year against an $8.9 billion shortfall in 1995.
"The current account deficit widened because the trade deficit worsened due to sluggish exports while the invisible trade deficit persisted," a statement from the bank said.

Meanwhile, domestic consumption, seen as one of the few bright spots in the economy, slowed. Wholesale sales gained 4.6 percent year-on-year in September compared with a 5.9 percent rise a year earlier.
Inflation also edged up with the consumer price index gaining 5.1 percent in October on the year, up from a 4.4 percent rise a year earlier.
The government has targeted inflation at below 5.0 percent this year.
On Tuesday the government's leading economic think tank, the Korea Development Institute, lowered its forecast for this year's gross domestic product (GDP) growth to 6.8 percent from 7.2 percent.

Private research institutes are dropping their forecasts even lower, raising a flurry of media speculation over whether South Korea can achieve a soft landing after heady growth of around 9.0 percent since the late 1980s.

September's trade deficit ballooned to $812.9 million, against a shortfall of $295.9 million a year earlier, and for the year to September it soared to $10.84 billion from $5.11 billion, the Bank of Korea said.
South Korea has been badly hurt by the yen's weakness against the U.S. dollar, which erodes its export competitiveness, and plunging world prices for semiconductors.
The yen has depreciated by 9.5 percent against the dollar this year, while the won has lost 7.2 percent.

"The weak yen is a really a big issue as Japanese exports are the major rivals for Korean exporters all over the world," said Ohn Ki-un, a senior fellow at the Korea Institute for International Economics and Trade.
The National Statistical Office said industrial inventories rose by 20.4 percent year-on-year in September, this year's second-biggest growth after a 20.9 percent rise in June.
Semiconductors and automobiles were the main culprits. Inventories for electronics parts, including semiconductors, were up 112.7 percent year-on-year and those for automobiles rose 43.1 percent.
"Companies will seriously suffer from high inventories and a growing burden for interest payments on dollar-denominated loans because of the strong dollar," said Ohn.
Industrial output grew 7.3 percent year-on-year in September against a 11.5 percent gain a year earlier, and ex-factory shipments rose 5.1 percent versus growth of 12.7 percent growth a year ago.
